title: Minimum Swap Cost So A Differs From B
statement:
You are given two arrays `A` and `B`, each of length `n`, using **1-based** indexing. Array `B` never changes. You may perform the following operation on `A` any number of times: choose two indices `i ≠ j` and swap `A[i]` with `A[j]`. This operation costs `i + j`.

Find the **minimum total cost** needed to transform `A` so that `A[i] ≠ B[i]` for every index `i` from `1` to `n`. If it is impossible, print `-1`.

If `A` already satisfies the condition, the cost is `0`.
input_format:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers `A[1] ... A[n]`.
The third line contains `n` integers `B[1] ... B[n]`.
output_format: Print a single integer: the minimum total cost, or `-1` if it is impossible.

examples.explanation: Positions 1, 3 and 5 are bad (A[i] = B[i]). Swap(1, 3) costs 4 and gives A = [3, 5, 1, 5, 5]; swap(1, 5) costs 6 and gives A = [5, 5, 1, 5, 3]. Now A differs from B everywhere, and the total cost is 4 + 6 = 10, which is the minimum.

Bad positions are 1, 2 and 5, holding the values 2, 2 and 3. Two 2s cannot fix each other, so one of them needs a helper from a good position whose A and B are both different from 2: position 3 qualifies (A = 1, B = 3). Swap(1, 3) costs 4 and swap(2, 5) costs 7, for a total of 11.
Every position is bad and every swap exchanges two equal values, so A can never change.

hints: Call an index bad if A[i] = B[i]. Every bad index must take part in at least one swap, so the cost is at least the sum of the bad indices. A good index only needs to be touched if it helps.

Two bad indices holding different values can fix each other with one swap. Trouble only arises when one value x occupies more than half of the bad indices: those extra copies of x need helpers from good indices p with A[p] ≠ x and B[p] ≠ x. Take the cheapest (smallest index) helpers.

If the bad indices are balanced but there is an odd number of them, one index is left without a partner. Check what the cheapest way to absorb it is; index 1 plays a special role because it is the cheapest index there is.
reference:
import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    n = int(data[0])
    A = data[1:1 + n]
    B = data[1 + n:1 + 2 * n]
    cnt = {}
    base = 0
    m = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if A[i] == B[i]:
            m += 1
            base += i + 1
            cnt[A[i]] = cnt.get(A[i], 0) + 1
    if m == 0:
        print(0)
        return
    x = max(cnt, key=lambda v: cnt[v])
    e = 2 * cnt[x] - m
    if e <= 0:
        print(base if m % 2 == 0 else base + 1)
        return
    tot = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if A[i] != B[i] and A[i] != x and B[i] != x:
            tot += i + 1
            e -= 1
            if e == 0:
                print(base + tot)
                return
    print(-1)

main()
